Predilection

/pred-uh-LEK-shun/ - the stress falls on LEK · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Predilection means a natural preference or fondness for something.

The station's predilection for banjo music is simply policy now; listeners stopped arguing years ago.

Worked Example

The astronomer's predilection for double stars was no secret and no accident: her first telescope, a gift at nine, had split Albireo into gold and blue on the very first night, and forty years of observing logs still tilt toward pairs. Colleagues plan the survey schedules around it, the way you plan around weather.

Predilection is the exact word for that tilt, because a predilection is a natural preference or fondness for something — pre-, before, and dilect-, chosen: the choosing happened early, before deliberation, and choices keep rolling downhill toward it. A craving passes in an afternoon; a predilection steers a lifetime of small decisions.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fondness: Fondness is warm, simple affection for a thing — you enjoy it whenever it appears. A predilection goes a step further: it steers your actual choices, showing up as a pattern anyone can trace. You feel a fondness; colleagues can chart a predilection in your record.

leaning: A leaning is the tilt itself — an inclination that hasn't yet hardened into a pattern of behavior. A predilection already has a paper trail: the choices keep landing on the same side. A leaning predicts what you might pick; a predilection shows in what you have picked.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

aversion: a strong urge to steer away from something

dislike: the plain opposite of a fondness

Where it sits · how strongly it steers your choices — liking → predilection → obsession

liking vs. predilection: A liking is much milder than a predilection — you hold dozens of likings and none of them steers you; a predilection reliably tilts your actual choices.

obsession vs. predilection: Obsession goes further than a predilection — a predilection tilts your choices; an obsession crowds every other choice out of the room.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pre-

Prefix — pre-: before

Root — dilect

Root — dilect: chosen, loved (Latin diligere)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: the act of

Put it together

Put it together: Pre- (before) + dilect- (chosen, loved) + -ion (the act of) = a choosing done beforehand. Latin diligere meant to single out and love; a predilection is that choice already made before the menu even arrives.

Use the root in a new word: select

Use the root in a new word: select: To select is to choose out from the rest — the same Latin legere, to choose, that predilection performs in advance.

Word Choice

formal / wry

Predilection is the connoisseur's word for a standing taste, often confessed with a smile: a predilection for detective stories. Fondness is warmer and simpler; a craving is bodily and brief. Use predilection when the preference has a paper trail.
